nodes.description: Rust async/await builds on zero-cost state machines — when you write async fn, the compiler generates a state machine, not threads.
contexts: set up Rust Axum web server with tokio and tower middleware
nodes.canonical_question: You have a Rust async function that makes two independent HTTP calls. Right now they run sequentially. How would you run them concurrently, and what is the difference between join! and select!, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: tokio::join! runs both futures concurrently and waits for both to complete, collecting both results. tokio::select! waits for whichever resolves first and cancels the other. For two independent calls where you need both results, join! is correct. Note that join! does not parallelise by itself — both futures share the same thread unless you use tokio::spawn to move them onto the thread pool.

nodes.description: The async executor that drives Rust futures — manages the thread pool and event loop.
contexts: set up Rust Axum web server with tokio and tower middleware
nodes.canonical_question: You add #[tokio::main] to your main function. What does it actually do, and what is the difference between the current_thread and multi_thread flavours, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: #[tokio::main] is a procedural macro that creates a tokio Runtime and calls block_on on your async main future. current_thread runs everything on a single thread — useful for lightweight apps or when you need single-threaded guarantees. multi_thread (the default) spawns a thread pool sized to your CPU cores and work-steals across them, giving true parallelism for CPU-bound tasks.

nodes.description: A Rust web framework built on hyper and tower — composable routing with extractors and type-safe middleware.
contexts: set up Rust Axum web server with tokio and tower middleware
nodes.canonical_question: You want to add request logging to every route in Axum. What is the difference between a tower Layer and a tower Service, and how do they compose in Axum, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: A Service is the core abstraction: it takes a request and returns a future that resolves to a response. A Layer wraps a Service to add cross-cutting behaviour — logging, auth checks, timeouts. Router::layer applies a tower Layer to all routes, stacking middlewares in declaration order. This is why Axum middleware is interoperable with the entire tower ecosystem.

nodes.description: Async database driver for Rust with compile-time query checking — PgPool manages a pool of reusable PostgreSQL connections.
contexts: add PostgreSQL with sqlx — migrations, connection pool, CRUD queries
nodes.canonical_question: Your Axum service acquires a database connection on every request. Under high load you start seeing timeouts. What does PgPool do, and what two numbers would you tune first, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: PgPool maintains a set of open connections that handlers borrow and return rather than open and close per request. The two most important tuning knobs are max_connections (cap on simultaneous live connections — too high overloads Postgres, too low starves handlers) and connect_timeout (how long a request waits before failing when the pool is exhausted). Watching pool wait time in your metrics tells you which limit you are hitting.

nodes.description: Versioned, incremental changes to your database schema — tracked so they apply once and in order across all environments.
contexts: add PostgreSQL with sqlx — migrations, connection pool, CRUD queries
nodes.canonical_question: You add a NOT NULL column to a production table that already has rows. What happens if you run the migration without a default, and how would you do this safely with zero downtime, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: Without a default, adding a NOT NULL column to a table with existing rows fails immediately — existing rows cannot satisfy the constraint. The safe path is three migrations: first add the column as nullable, then backfill existing rows with a default value, then add the NOT NULL constraint. On large tables the backfill should be batched to avoid a full-table lock.

nodes.description: Stateless token-based auth where the server signs a payload the client stores and sends back on every request.
contexts: implement JWT authentication with refresh token rotation
nodes.canonical_question: You are issuing JWTs with a 15-minute expiry. A user is halfway through a checkout flow when their token expires. What needs to happen on both sides for the experience to feel seamless, without storing session state on the server, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: The client stores a long-lived refresh token (ideally in an httpOnly cookie) and a short-lived access token in memory. When the access token expires, the client silently posts the refresh token to a dedicated endpoint. The server validates the refresh token against a stored record, issues a new access token (and rotates the refresh token to prevent reuse), and the original request retries transparently. The server stays stateless for access tokens while retaining revocation control via the refresh token record.

nodes.description: Cookies with the HttpOnly flag cannot be read by JavaScript — only sent by the browser automatically on requests to the matching domain.
contexts: implement JWT authentication with refresh token rotation
nodes.canonical_question: A colleague suggests storing the refresh token in localStorage for easier JavaScript access. What attack does httpOnly prevent that localStorage does not, and what does it not protect against, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: httpOnly prevents XSS from reading the cookie value via document.cookie or fetch — a malicious script injected into the page cannot exfiltrate the refresh token. localStorage has no such protection. However, httpOnly does not protect against CSRF: the browser still sends the cookie automatically on cross-origin requests. You still need SameSite=Strict or a CSRF token for that. httpOnly and CSRF protection address different threat models and you need both.

nodes.description: Managing the lifecycle of short-lived access tokens and long-lived refresh tokens to maintain seamless sessions.
contexts: implement JWT authentication with refresh token rotation
nodes.canonical_question: Your refresh tokens have a 7-day expiry. A user is active every day. Should their session ever expire, and how does token rotation affect this, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: With rotation, each use of a refresh token issues a new one, resetting the expiry window. An active user effectively has a rolling session that never expires as long as they use the app within 7 days. The session only terminates if they are inactive for the full expiry window, if they log out explicitly, or if the server revokes the token family. This is a deliberate UX trade-off — you get long sessions without storing them server-side, at the cost of a slightly larger attack window if a refresh token is stolen.

nodes.description: Time-based automatic key removal in Redis — keys expire and are deleted after a configured duration.
contexts: add Redis caching layer with TTL-based invalidation
nodes.canonical_question: You cache user profile data with a 5-minute TTL. A user updates their email and the old value is served for up to 5 minutes. How would you make the cache consistent without switching to write-through, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: On profile update, explicitly delete the cache key (cache-aside invalidation). The next request will miss and repopulate from the database with fresh data. This avoids the stale window without requiring you to write to the cache on every mutation. The trade-off is a single cold miss after each update rather than a guaranteed stale serve window — which is usually the right call for user-visible data.

nodes.description: Approaches for keeping a cache consistent with its source of truth — write-through, cache-aside, TTL expiry, and explicit invalidation.
contexts: add Redis caching layer with TTL-based invalidation
nodes.canonical_question: You have write-through caching. A database write succeeds but the cache update fails. What is the consistency state, and how would you handle it, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: The cache now holds stale data while the database has the correct value — readers will see the old value until the TTL expires or an explicit invalidation happens. The safest remediation is to delete the cache key on any write failure rather than leave it stale, accepting a cold miss on the next read. For critical paths, a transactional outbox pattern or a message queue can make cache invalidation durable and retryable.

nodes.description: A Redis data structure mapping member strings to floating-point scores — ordered by score, O(log N) insert and rank queries.
contexts: implement rate limiting with Redis sorted sets and Lua scripting
nodes.canonical_question: You are implementing a sliding-window rate limiter using a Redis sorted set with request timestamps as scores. Walk through the operations you need per incoming request, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: On each request: ZREMRANGEBYSCORE to remove entries older than the window boundary, ZCARD to count remaining entries (the current request count), and if under the limit, ZADD with the current timestamp as the score. These three operations must be atomic — a race between ZCARD and ZADD from concurrent requests could let both through. Wrapping them in a Lua script guarantees atomicity without a MULTI/EXEC round-trip.

nodes.description: Redis executes Lua scripts atomically — the entire script runs as a single operation, preventing race conditions.
contexts: implement rate limiting with Redis sorted sets and Lua scripting
nodes.canonical_question: A Lua script in Redis blocks the event loop for the duration of its execution. What does this mean for your rate limiter script, and how do you mitigate it, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: Because Redis is single-threaded and Lua scripts run atomically, a slow or infinite Lua script blocks every other Redis command for the duration. For a rate limiter, the script is a fixed few operations (remove stale entries, count, conditionally insert) and completes in microseconds — acceptable in practice. Mitigation for longer scripts: keep them short and deterministic, never do I/O inside Lua, and set lua-time-limit in redis.conf to kill runaway scripts.

nodes.description: Build stages that produce smaller final images by discarding build tools and dev dependencies.
contexts: backfill: feat: Docker multi-stage build
nodes.canonical_question: Your Rust Docker image is 1.8 GB. You switch to a multi-stage build with a rust:slim builder and a debian:slim final stage. What ends up in the final image, and why is the size so much smaller, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: The final image contains only the compiled binary and its runtime dependencies — no Rust toolchain, no source code, no cargo registry cache. The builder stage installs the compiler, fetches crates, and produces the binary; the final stage copies only that artifact. Rust binaries are statically linked by default (with musl) so you can even use a scratch base image with zero OS overhead. The reduction from ~1.8 GB to ~20 MB is typical.

nodes.description: Techniques to reduce Docker image size — multi-stage builds, .dockerignore, minimal base images.
contexts: backfill: feat: Docker multi-stage build
nodes.canonical_question: You have a .dockerignore file but your image is still large. List three other levers you would pull to reduce image size, in order of likely impact, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: First, switch to a minimal base image (debian:slim or alpine instead of ubuntu). Second, chain RUN commands with && to prevent intermediate layer bloat — each RUN creates a layer, and apt-get install followed by a separate apt-get clean does not shrink the previous layer. Third, use multi-stage builds to leave build tools behind. Beyond that: remove man pages and documentation inside the image, and use --no-install-recommends with apt-get.

nodes.description: YAML-based CI/CD pipeline definition — jobs, steps, runners, secrets, matrix builds.
contexts: backfill: ci: add GitHub Actions workflow
nodes.canonical_question: Your GitHub Actions workflow runs tests on every push. Cargo dependency downloads are taking 4 minutes. How do you cache them, and what cache key would you use, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: Use the actions/cache action targeting ~/.cargo/registry, ~/.cargo/git, and ./target. The cache key should include the OS, a static prefix, and a hash of Cargo.lock — for example: ${{ runner.os }}-cargo-${{ hashFiles('**/Cargo.lock') }}. This gives a precise hit when dependencies have not changed and a miss (triggering a fresh download and cache save) only when Cargo.lock changes. A restore-keys fallback on just the OS prefix avoids a full cold start when the lock file changes.

nodes.description: Automated build, test, and deploy pipelines — fast feedback loops, environment promotion, rollback.
contexts: backfill: ci: add GitHub Actions workflow
nodes.canonical_question: Your pipeline deploys to production on every merge to main. A bad deploy goes out at 2am. What does a good rollback story look like, and what pipeline features make it fast, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: A fast rollback requires knowing the previous known-good artifact (image tag or binary hash) and having a deploy step that can re-point production to it in seconds. Concretely: tag every build with the git SHA, keep the previous deploy artifact accessible (do not overwrite), and have a manual trigger in the pipeline that re-runs the deploy step with a specific tag. Blue/green or canary deployments reduce blast radius further by keeping the previous version warm before cutting over fully.

nodes.description: Machine-readable REST API description format — enables client generation, interactive docs, and contract testing.
contexts: backfill: docs: add OpenAPI spec and Swagger UI
nodes.canonical_question: You hand a client team your OpenAPI spec and they generate a typed SDK from it. Three weeks later you add a required field to a response. What breaks, and how do you version this safely, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: Adding a required field to a response is a breaking change for any client that has generated a strict deserializer — unexpected fields may be fine, but a field the SDK expects to always be present now being absent (for old records) will cause parse failures. Safe versioning: treat the spec as a contract, use semantic versioning on the spec itself, and for breaking changes either version the API path (/v2/tasks) or use content negotiation. Additive changes (new optional fields) are generally backward-compatible.

nodes.description: Reading and normalising delimited text files — handling encoding issues, inconsistent quoting, and missing headers.
contexts: backfill: Initial commit: Enhanced home banking system
nodes.canonical_question: Your CSV parser works on sample files but fails silently on production exports from a different bank. What are the three most common CSV format variations that break naive parsers, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: The three most common culprits are: (1) encoding — files from older banking software are often ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252, not UTF-8, causing silent garbling or errors on special characters like pound signs and accented letters; (2) quoting inconsistency — some exporters quote every field, some only fields containing commas, and some use single quotes instead of double quotes; (3) header row presence and naming — some exports include a header, some do not, and column names differ by bank. Sniff encoding with chardet, use a robust CSV library, and validate column count and types before processing.

nodes.description: Classifying financial transactions into categories (groceries, utilities, salary) using rule-based or ML approaches.
contexts: backfill: Initial commit: Enhanced home banking system
nodes.canonical_question: You are building a rule-based categoriser that matches transaction descriptions to categories. A supermarket chain has 40 different description formats across branches. What is a better architecture than a list of string equality checks, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: Use a priority-ordered list of regex patterns, each mapped to a category. Group patterns by merchant type so the supermarket group matches any of its 40 variants with one pattern. Store rules in a config file rather than code so non-engineers can add rules. Add a confidence score — exact merchant name matches score higher than partial matches — so you can flag low-confidence categorisations for manual review. For volume, compile all regexes once at startup rather than recompiling per transaction.

nodes.description: In-memory tabular data manipulation — filtering, grouping, merging, and transforming rows and columns.
contexts: backfill: feat: Add transaction categorization script and processing functions
nodes.canonical_question: You are groupby-aggregating 500k transaction rows and it takes 8 seconds. You have not changed the algorithm. What three things would you check first, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: First, check dtypes — groupby on an object column (string) is significantly slower than on a categorical; converting high-cardinality string columns with astype('category') often gives a 2-5x speedup. Second, check if you are doing the groupby on a copy versus a view — unnecessary copies inflate memory and slow everything down. Third, look at what you are doing inside the aggregation: custom apply functions with Python lambdas are slow; switching to built-in agg functions (sum, mean, count) uses optimised C paths. If none of those help, consider Polars for large frame operations.

nodes.description: Every financial transaction has equal debits and credits across accounts — the accounting identity that makes books balance.
contexts: backfill: Initial commit: Enhanced home banking system
nodes.canonical_question: You record a £200 grocery payment from a current account in a double-entry system. What are the two journal entries, and which accounts do they affect, question?
nodes.canonical_answer: Debit the Groceries expense account by £200 (expenses increase with a debit), and credit the Current Account asset account by £200 (assets decrease with a credit). The net effect is zero — the accounting equation stays balanced. In a data pipeline, this means every import row generates two ledger rows; a sum of all amounts across all accounts should always equal zero, which is a useful invariant to assert after each import.
